facts.text: An abacus is a counting tool in which beads are moved along rods set in a frame.
A crossbar divides the Chinese abacus (suanpan); each rod has two beads above the bar and five beads below it.
On the Chinese abacus, a bead above the bar stands for five and a bead below the bar stands for one.
The abacus was used in China for many centuries, and a related form, the soroban, became common in Japan.
Desktop electronic calculators appeared in the early 1960s; these early machines were heavy and costly before lighter, cheaper models replaced them.
Handheld electronic calculators reached the U.S. market in 1970 and 1971.
Handheld calculators were battery-powered and could do basic arithmetic such as adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing.
Prices of handheld calculators were high at first (for example, 395 dollars for one 1972 model) but fell sharply during the 1970s as better chips and displays were developed.
In abacus-based mental calculation training, children first learn on a real abacus and later calculate by picturing the beads of an imaginary abacus in their minds.
